Atomic Structure.intro: Atoms are made of protons, neutrons and electrons. Understanding the structure of atoms and how it relates to radioactivity is the foundation of P4.
Atomic Structure.mnemonic: "Protons Plus Neutrons live in the Nucleus; Electrons Exist Everywhere outside" — or remember charges: Protons Positive, Neutrons Neutral, Electrons (–).

sections.title: Structure of the Atom
sections.text: An atom has a tiny dense nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in energy levels (shells). Atoms are mostly empty space.
points: Nucleus — protons (charge +1, mass 1) + neutrons (charge 0, mass 1); tiny and dense; positively charged
Electrons — charge −1, mass ~1/2000 of proton; orbit in shells at specific energy levels
Neutral atom — number of protons = number of electrons; overall charge = 0
Atomic number (Z) — number of protons; defines the element; same for all atoms of that element
Mass number (A) — protons + neutrons; number of neutrons = A − Z

sections.title: Isotopes and Ions
sections.text: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. Ions are atoms that have gained or lost electrons.
points: Isotopes — same element (same protons), different number of neutrons; same chemical properties; different mass
Radioactive isotopes — unstable nuclei; spontaneously emit radiation to become more stable
Ions — atoms that have gained electrons (negative ion) or lost electrons (positive ion)
Notation — ₂⁶C means mass number 12, atomic number 6 (carbon-12); neutrons = 12 − 6 = 6
Size — atom diameter ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m; nucleus diameter ≈ 10⁻¹⁴ m; atom is mostly empty space

sections.title: Charges and Masses Summary
sections.text: The sub-atomic particles have specific relative charges and masses that determine atomic properties.
points: Proton — relative charge: +1; relative mass: 1; found in nucleus
Neutron — relative charge: 0; relative mass: 1; found in nucleus
Electron — relative charge: −1; relative mass: 1/2000 (negligible); found in shells
Nucleus charge — always positive (only protons and neutrons); equal to atomic number × (+1)
Almost all the mass — protons and neutrons account for >99.9% of the atom's total mass

keyTerms.def: Number of protons in the nucleus — defines the element
Total protons + neutrons in the nucleus
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
An atom that has gained or lost electrons — has an electric charge
The tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons
Fixed energy level around the nucleus where electrons are found

examTips: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number. AQA frequently asks you to calculate the number of neutrons from the notation. Practice this calculation.
Isotopes: same number of protons (same element), different number of neutrons (different mass). They have identical chemical properties but different physical properties.
Ions: same protons and neutrons as the original atom, but different number of electrons. A positive ion has FEWER electrons; a negative ion has MORE electrons.
commonMistakes: Saying isotopes have different chemical properties — they have the SAME chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons and protons.
Confusing isotopes (different neutrons) with ions (different electrons) — isotopes change the nucleus; ions change the electron count.
Saying the mass of an electron is zero — it is approximately 1/2000 of the mass of a proton, so it is negligible but not zero.
clozePassages: An atom has a small, dense nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in shells. The nucleus is positively charged. Protons have a positive charge of +1. Neutrons have no charge. Electrons have a negative charge of -1 and a negligible mass. The number of protons equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom. The atomic number equals the number of protons.

The mass number of an atom is the total number of protons and neutrons. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. They have the same chemical properties but different physical properties and different stabilities. Some isotopes are radioactive — they have unstable nuclei that decay spontaneously, emitting radiation. The decay of radioactive isotopes is random and cannot be predicted for individual atoms.

Most of an atom is empty space. The nucleus is approximately 10,000 times smaller than the atom itself. The diameter of an atom is about 10⁻¹⁰ m; the nucleus is about 10⁻¹⁴ m. Despite being so small, the nucleus contains almost all of the atom's mass. This understanding came from Rutherford's gold foil experiment, which showed that most alpha particles passed straight through the foil rather than being deflected.

History of the Atom.intro: Our model of the atom has changed over time as new experimental evidence has emerged. This is a key example of how science works.
History of the Atom.mnemonic: "Dalton's Tiny Round ball, Thomson's Pudding, Rutherford's nuclear Ring, Bohr's orbit — DTRB" — Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr.

sections.title: Development of Atomic Models
sections.text: Scientific models of the atom have developed over 200 years as new experimental evidence required existing models to be revised or replaced.
numbered: Dalton (1803) — indivisible solid spheres; atoms are the smallest particles of matter
Thomson (1904) — plum pudding: electrons embedded in a diffuse positive sphere of charge
Rutherford (1911) — nuclear model: small dense positive nucleus; electrons orbit around it; atom mostly empty
Bohr (1913) — electrons in fixed circular orbits at specific energy levels; electrons can jump between levels
Modern quantum model — electrons in probability clouds (orbitals); position cannot be precisely known
points: Dalton (1803) — indivisible solid spheres; atoms are the smallest particles of matter
Thomson (1904) — plum pudding: electrons embedded in a diffuse positive sphere of charge
Rutherford (1911) — nuclear model: small dense positive nucleus; electrons orbit around it; atom mostly empty
Bohr (1913) — electrons in fixed circular orbits at specific energy levels
Modern quantum model — electrons in probability clouds; position cannot be precisely known

sections.title: Rutherford's Alpha Scattering Experiment
sections.text: Rutherford's gold foil experiment provided evidence for the nuclear model, disproving the plum pudding model by showing the nucleus is a tiny concentrated positive charge.
points: Setup — alpha particles fired at a very thin gold foil; detected on a screen surrounding the foil
Most passed straight through — atom is mostly empty space
Small fraction deflected at large angles — small, dense, positively charged nucleus exists
Very few bounced back (>90°) — nucleus is extremely small relative to atom size
Disproved plum pudding — positive charge is NOT spread out; it is concentrated in a tiny nucleus

callout.label: Why it Disproved Plum Pudding
callout.text: The plum pudding model predicted all alpha particles should pass through with small deflections. The large-angle deflections could only be explained by a concentrated positive charge (nucleus).

sections.title: How Science Develops
sections.text: The history of the atom illustrates how scientific models are revised when new evidence cannot be explained by the existing model.
points: Evidence drives change — Thomson's discovery of the electron disproved Dalton; Rutherford's results disproved Thomson
Peer review — new models must be tested and accepted by the scientific community
Bohr's refinement — added fixed energy levels to explain atomic emission spectra
Emission spectra — each element produces a unique spectrum; explained by electrons dropping between energy levels
Modern model — quantum mechanics replaced Bohr's circular orbits with probability clouds

keyTerms.def: Thomson's model: electrons embedded in a diffuse positive sphere of charge
Rutherford's model: small dense positive nucleus surrounded by orbiting electrons
Positively charged particle (2 protons + 2 neutrons) emitted in radioactive decay; used in Rutherford's experiment
A fixed orbit or shell at which electrons can exist around the nucleus (Bohr model)
Unique pattern of light frequencies emitted by an element when electrons drop to lower energy levels
Rutherford's 1911 experiment that provided evidence for the nuclear model of the atom

examTips: Rutherford's results: most pass through = atom is mostly empty space; large-angle deflections = small dense positive nucleus. Link each observation to its conclusion — AQA mark schemes require both.
Scientific models change when new evidence cannot be explained by the existing model. The plum pudding model was replaced, not just updated — this is a key point for 'how science works' questions.
Know the order: Dalton → Thomson (plum pudding) → Rutherford (nuclear) → Bohr (energy levels) → modern quantum model.
commonMistakes: Saying Rutherford's experiment confirmed the plum pudding model — it DISPROVED it. The large deflections could not be explained by the plum pudding model.
Forgetting to explain what each observation tells us about atomic structure — 'most passed through' alone is not enough; you must say what it means (mostly empty space).
Confusing Thomson's discovery (electrons) with Rutherford's discovery (nucleus) — Thomson found the electron; Rutherford found the nucleus.
clozePassages: The model of the atom has evolved over time as new evidence emerged. Dalton proposed atoms were solid indivisible spheres. Thomson discovered the electron and proposed the plum pudding model with electrons embedded in a positive sphere. Rutherford's gold foil experiment showed the atom has a tiny positive nucleus. Bohr proposed electrons orbit in fixed shells. Modern models treat electrons as probability clouds.

Rutherford's gold foil experiment was crucial in developing the nuclear model of the atom. Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil, but some were deflected and a few bounced straight back. This proved the atom is mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus. The plum pudding model predicted that all particles would pass through with minimal deflection, so the results were surprising and led to a revolution in atomic theory.

Niels Bohr refined Rutherford's model by proposing that electrons occupy fixed energy levels or shells. Electrons can only exist at specific energies and can move between shells by absorbing or emitting photons of light. When electrons drop to a lower energy level, they emit light of a specific frequency, producing atomic emission spectra. These spectra are unique to each element and can be used to identify elements in distant stars.

Radioactive Decay.intro: Some atomic nuclei are unstable and spontaneously emit radiation. This is radioactive decay — it is random and cannot be controlled.
Radioactive Decay.mnemonic: "Alpha Blocks Paper; Beta Blocks Aluminium; Gamma needs Lead Guards" — ABP, BAL, GLG for stopping materials. Or: 'Alpha is A-mazing at ionising but stopped by A sheet of paper'.

sections.title: Types of Nuclear Radiation
sections.text: There are three main types of nuclear radiation: alpha, beta and gamma. They differ in mass, charge, ionising power and penetrating ability.
points: Alpha (α) — 2 protons + 2 neutrons (helium nucleus); charge +2; highly ionising; range ~5 cm in air; stopped by paper or skin
Beta (β) — fast electron from nucleus (neutron → proton + electron); charge −1; moderately ionising; stopped by a few mm aluminium
Gamma (γ) — electromagnetic wave (high frequency); no charge, no mass; weakly ionising; needs thick lead or metres of concrete
Ionising power vs penetrating ability — these are INVERSELY related: α most ionising/least penetrating; γ least ionising/most penetrating
Deflection in fields — α deflected towards negative plate; β deflected towards positive plate; γ not deflected

sections.title: Nuclear Equations
sections.text: Nuclear equations show the changes to proton and mass numbers during radioactive decay. Both must be conserved (balanced).
points: Alpha decay — mass number decreases by 4, atomic number decreases by 2; e.g. ²³⁸U → ²³⁴Th + ⁴He
Beta decay — mass number UNCHANGED; atomic number increases by 1 (neutron converts to proton + electron)
Gamma decay — no change to mass number or atomic number; only energy is released
Balancing equations — top numbers (mass) must add up on both sides; bottom numbers (atomic) must add up on both sides
Beta notation — beta particle written as ⁰₋₁e in nuclear equations

sections.title: Properties Comparison
sections.text: A summary of key properties helps to compare the three types of radiation for exam questions.

callout.label: Summary Table
callout.text: α: most ionising, least penetrating. γ: least ionising, most penetrating. β: in between. Ionising power and penetrating ability are INVERSELY related.

points: Nature — α: helium nucleus; β: electron; γ: electromagnetic wave
Charge — α: +2; β: −1; γ: 0
Stopped by — α: paper/skin; β: aluminium (few mm); γ: thick lead/concrete
Ionising power — α: highest (creates most ion pairs per cm); γ: lowest
Speed — α: slowest (~10% speed of light); β: ~90% c; γ: speed of light (c)

keyTerms.def: Spontaneous emission of radiation from unstable nuclei — random and cannot be controlled
2 protons + 2 neutrons (helium nucleus); charge +2; highly ionising; stopped by paper
High-speed electron emitted from nucleus when neutron converts to proton; stopped by aluminium
High-frequency electromagnetic wave from nucleus; no charge or mass; needs lead to absorb
Radiation that removes electrons from atoms, creating ions — can damage living cells
An equation showing radioactive decay with conservation of mass number and atomic number

examTips: α: most ionising, stopped by paper. β: stopped by a few mm of aluminium. γ: stopped by thick lead or concrete. AQA frequently asks which type of radiation is most suitable for a specific use — match penetrating ability to the application.
Radioactive decay is random and spontaneous — it CANNOT be affected by temperature, pressure, chemical state, or any external factor. AQA may ask you to explain this.
For nuclear equations: mass numbers (top) and atomic numbers (bottom) must balance on both sides. Practice writing and checking equations for alpha, beta, and gamma decay.
commonMistakes: Saying beta particles are protons — they are ELECTRONS emitted from the nucleus when a neutron converts to a proton.
Confusing ionising power and penetrating ability — they are inversely related. Alpha is MOST ionising but LEAST penetrating.
Forgetting that gamma decay causes no change to mass or atomic number — only energy is released.
clozePassages: Radioactive decay occurs when an unstable nucleus emits radiation to become more stable. Alpha decay emits a helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons) — the mass number decreases by 4 and atomic number by 2. Beta decay emits an electron from the nucleus when a neutron converts to a proton — atomic number increases by 1. Gamma decay emits electromagnetic radiation and causes no change in mass or atomic number.

Alpha (α) particles are helium nuclei with high ionising power but low penetration — stopped by a few centimetres of air or thin paper. Beta (β) particles are fast electrons with medium ionising power — stopped by a few mm of aluminium. Gamma (γ) rays are electromagnetic waves with low ionising power but high penetration — reduced but not stopped by thick lead or concrete. The ionising power is related to how strongly each type interacts with matter.

Nuclear equations show radioactive decay with conservation of mass number and atomic number. In alpha decay: ²³⁸U → ²³⁴Th + ⁴He. In beta decay: ¹⁴C → ¹⁴N + ⁰e (electron). Gamma radiation accompanies alpha and beta decay and carries no charge or mass. Nuclear equations must balance — the total mass number and total atomic number must be the same on both sides of the equation.

Nuclear Radiation.intro: Nuclear radiation can be both harmful and beneficial. Understanding the risks and uses is important for P4.
Nuclear Radiation.mnemonic: "Good tracers are Gamma with a Short half-life" — G for Gamma (penetrates body), S for Short half-life (decays quickly, reduces patient dose).

sections.title: Detecting Radiation
sections.text: Ionising radiation can be detected because it causes ionisation in detectors. The most common detectors are Geiger-Müller tubes and photographic film.
points: Geiger-Müller (GM) tube — detects ionising radiation; each particle triggers a brief electrical pulse counted by a ratemeter
Photographic film badge — used by radiation workers; film darkens with exposure; shows accumulated dose over time
Count rate — number of counts per second (cps) or per minute (cpm); measure of activity
Background correction — always subtract background count rate from measured count rate in experiments
Background sources — cosmic rays, radon gas (rocks), food, medical uses; UK average ~2.7 mSv/year

sections.title: Uses of Radiation
sections.text: Radiation has many beneficial uses in medicine, industry and everyday life. The type of radiation chosen depends on its properties.
points: Medical tracers — gamma emitters (e.g. technetium-99m) injected into body; detected outside by gamma camera; must have short half-life
Cancer radiotherapy — focused gamma beams destroy tumour cells; surrounding tissue minimised
Sterilisation — gamma radiation kills bacteria in medical equipment without using heat
Smoke detectors — alpha source (americium-241) ionises air; smoke disrupts ion current; triggers alarm
Thickness gauges — beta particles used to monitor paper or metal thickness; thicker material absorbs more beta

sections.title: Background Radiation
sections.text: Background radiation is always present from natural and artificial sources. It must be accounted for in all radiation experiments.
points: Natural sources — radon gas (from granite rocks), cosmic rays from space, radioactive elements in food and water
Artificial sources — nuclear industry, medical scans, nuclear weapons testing fallout
Radon gas — main source of background radiation in UK; higher in areas with granite (e.g. Cornwall)
Must subtract background — corrected count = measured count − background count; essential for accurate results
Dose and risk — measured in millisieverts (mSv); UK average ~2.7 mSv/year; varies by occupation and location

keyTerms.def: Low-level radiation always present from natural and artificial sources — must be subtracted in experiments
A radioactive substance introduced into the body to track a biological process; must be a gamma emitter with short half-life
Detector for ionising radiation — each ionising particle produces an electrical pulse
The number of radioactive decays detected per unit time (counts per second or per minute)
Exposure to radiation from an external source — person can move away; exposure ends when source removed
Radioactive material on or inside the body — ongoing internal exposure; more dangerous than irradiation

examTips: Always subtract background radiation in practical experiments — failure to do so will lose marks in AQA practicals questions.
Medical tracers must be: gamma emitter (so it can be detected outside the body) AND short half-life (so it decays quickly and reduces patient dose). Alpha is NEVER suitable as a tracer.

Smoke detectors use ALPHA sources — alpha ionises the air between two electrodes; smoke disrupts the ionisation current. AQA may ask why alpha is chosen here (most ionising = best at ionising the air gap).
commonMistakes: Forgetting to subtract background radiation in count rate calculations — this is a very common exam error.
Saying alpha is best for medical tracers — it is too ionising and CANNOT penetrate tissue to be detected outside the body.
Confusing irradiation (external source; ends when you move away) with contamination (source on/in body; continuous exposure).
clozePassages: The three main types of nuclear radiation are alpha, beta, and gamma. Alpha particles are the most ionising but least penetrating. They cause serious damage if the source is inside the body (contamination). Beta particles have intermediate ionising and penetrating properties. Gamma rays are the least ionising but most penetrating. All types of radiation can damage living cells by ionising molecules, potentially causing cancer or cell death.

Radiation can be detected using a Geiger-Müller tube connected to a counter. Each ionising particle entering the tube triggers a brief electrical pulse which is counted. Background radiation is always present and comes from natural sources (cosmic rays, radon gas, rocks, food) and artificial sources (nuclear industry, medical uses). Background radiation must be subtracted when measuring the activity of a radioactive source.

Irradiation is exposure to a radioactive source from outside the body. Contamination is when radioactive material enters the body or gets onto clothing and skin. Contamination is generally more dangerous because the source remains in close contact with tissues for extended periods. Protective measures include wearing lead aprons, keeping distance from sources, minimising exposure time, and wearing protective clothing to prevent contamination.

Half-life.intro: Half-life is the time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. It is constant for each radioactive isotope.
Half-life.mnemonic: "Half the heroes decay each round" — after each half-life, half the remaining nuclei have decayed. Start with 1000: after 1 half-life → 500; after 2 → 250; after 3 → 125.

sections.title: What is Half-life?
sections.text: Half-life is the time for the activity of a radioactive source to halve. It is constant for a given isotope and unaffected by external conditions.
points: Half-life — time for activity (or count rate) to halve; OR time for half the unstable nuclei to decay
Constant value — half-life is fixed for each isotope; cannot be changed by temperature, pressure or chemistry
Random process — impossible to predict which nucleus decays next; but statistics of large numbers are predictable
Exponential decay — activity never reaches exactly zero; gets smaller and smaller but never disappears
Range of half-lives — from fractions of a second (e.g. nitrogen-16: 7 s) to billions of years (e.g. uranium-238: 4.5 × 10⁹ years)

sections.title: Half-life Calculations
sections.text: After n half-lives, the remaining fraction of a radioactive sample is (1/2)ⁿ.

callout.label: Method
callout.text: After n half-lives: remaining fraction = (1/2)ⁿ. E.g. after 3 half-lives: 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8 remains. If initial count = 800 and half-life = 2 years: after 6 years (3 half-lives) → 100 counts.

points: Formula — remaining = initial × (1/2)ⁿ where n = number of half-lives elapsed
Finding n — n = total time ÷ half-life
Worked example — initial activity 640 Bq, half-life 5 years: after 20 years (4 half-lives): 640 × (1/2)⁴ = 640 ÷ 16 = 40 Bq
From graph — read off time when activity halves; that is the half-life
Units — activity measured in becquerels (Bq); 1 Bq = 1 decay per second

sections.title: Choosing Isotopes
sections.text: The half-life of an isotope determines its suitability for different applications.
points: Medical tracers — short half-life (hours to days) so patient dose is minimised; technetium-99m has t₁/₂ = 6 hours
Radiotherapy — longer half-life to deliver sustained dose to tumour
Long-term power — long half-life maintains constant power output (e.g. plutonium-238 in space probes: t₁/₂ = 87 years)
Carbon dating — carbon-14 (t₁/₂ = 5700 years) used to date organic material up to ~50 000 years old
Radioactive waste — must store for many half-lives; high-level waste stored for thousands of years

keyTerms.def: Time for the activity of a radioactive sample to halve (or for half the nuclei to decay)
The number of radioactive decays per second — measured in becquerels (Bq)
Unit of radioactive activity — 1 Bq = 1 decay per second
Activity halves in each successive equal time interval — curve never reaches zero
Using the known half-life of carbon-14 (5700 years) to determine the age of organic material
Measured count rate minus background count rate — gives activity due to source alone

examTips: From a graph: read off the activity at two points — the half-life is the time for activity to halve. Draw horizontal and vertical lines on the graph to show your working.
After n half-lives: remaining = original × (1/2)ⁿ. Make sure you calculate n = total time ÷ half-life first, then apply the formula.
The activity of a source NEVER reaches zero — it decreases exponentially. AQA may test this understanding directly.
commonMistakes: Saying after 2 half-lives, nothing remains — after 2 half-lives, 1/4 (25%) remains. After 10 half-lives there is still approximately 0.1% left.
Confusing half-life (time for activity to halve) with time for all nuclei to decay — a radioactive source never fully decays to zero activity.
Using the wrong time for n — always divide total elapsed time by the half-life to find n before calculating remaining activity.
clozePassages: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. It is also the time taken for the activity (count rate) of a source to halve. Half-life is constant for a given isotope and ranges from fractions of a second to billions of years. Radioactive decay is a random process — it is impossible to predict which individual nucleus will decay next, but the average behaviour of large numbers of nuclei is predictable.

The activity of a radioactive source decreases over time following an exponential decay pattern. After one half-life, activity halves. After two half-lives, activity is one quarter of the original. After three half-lives, it is one eighth, and so on. The half-life determines how long a radioactive material remains hazardous. Short-lived isotopes decay quickly to safe levels; long-lived isotopes such as plutonium remain radioactive for thousands of years.

Carbon dating uses the known half-life of carbon-14 (5700 years) to determine the age of organic materials. Living organisms maintain a constant ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12. After death, the carbon-14 decays without replacement. By measuring the remaining carbon-14, scientists can calculate when the organism died. Uranium-lead dating uses the decay of uranium-238 (half-life 4.5 billion years) to date ancient rocks.

Hazards.intro: Ionising radiation damages living cells and can cause cancer. Safe use of radiation requires understanding and minimising the risks.
Hazards.mnemonic: "Distance, Duration, Dense shielding (3 Ds) keep you safe" — increase Distance, decrease Duration of exposure, use Dense (lead) shielding.

sections.title: How Radiation Harms
sections.text: Ionising radiation is dangerous because it can remove electrons from atoms, creating ions that damage cells and DNA.
points: Ionisation — radiation removes electrons from atoms → ions formed → disrupts chemical bonds in cells
DNA damage — mutations in DNA can prevent normal cell division → cancer
High dose effects — radiation sickness, hair loss, nausea, cell death; lethal at very high doses
Low dose effects — increased long-term risk of cancer; no immediate symptoms
Dose measured in Sieverts (Sv) — accounts for both the amount and type of radiation; 1 Sv is very large, so mSv used

sections.title: Reducing Risk
sections.text: The three key principles for reducing radiation dose are: maximise distance, minimise time, use appropriate shielding.
points: Increase distance — intensity decreases with distance squared (inverse square law); stand well back from sources
Minimise exposure time — less time near source = less dose received
Shielding — lead aprons for gamma; thick walls of concrete in nuclear power stations; tongs to handle sources
Dosimeters/film badges — worn by radiation workers to monitor cumulative dose
ALARP principle — As Low As Reasonably Practicable; balance benefit of using radiation against risk

sections.title: Contamination vs Irradiation
sections.text: Irradiation and contamination are two different types of radiation exposure with very different risk levels.

callout.label: Key Distinction
callout.text: Irradiation = being exposed to radiation from a source outside the body. Contamination = radioactive material on or inside the body (more dangerous — continuous exposure).

points: Irradiation — external source; exposure stops when you move away or source is removed; less dangerous
Contamination — radioactive material on skin, clothing, or inhaled/ingested; source stays with person; more dangerous
Alpha inside body — most dangerous type of contamination; highly ionising at close range to tissues
Beta and gamma external — beta can cause skin burns; gamma penetrates and damages internal organs
Protective clothing — prevents skin contamination; respirators prevent inhalation of radioactive dust

keyTerms.def: Exposure to radiation from an external source — stops when source is removed or person moves away
Radioactive material on or inside the body — ongoing internal exposure; more dangerous than irradiation
Removal of electrons from atoms — mechanism by which radiation damages cells
Unit of radiation dose — accounts for both amount and biological effect of radiation
As Low As Reasonably Practicable — principle for minimising radiation dose in workplaces
Device worn by radiation workers to measure and monitor their cumulative radiation dose

examTips: Contamination is MORE dangerous than irradiation — the source stays with the person, giving continuous exposure. AQA frequently asks students to explain why contamination is more hazardous.
Alpha is most dangerous if ingested or inhaled (highly ionising inside body tissue) despite being stopped by skin externally. Beta causes skin burns. Gamma can penetrate to damage internal organs.
Three ways to reduce dose: increase distance, decrease time of exposure, use lead/concrete shielding. Know all three for AQA exam questions on radiation safety.
commonMistakes: Saying alpha is harmless because it's stopped by skin — inside the body (contamination), alpha is the MOST damaging type because it is highly ionising.
Confusing irradiation (external source, can step away) with contamination (source on/in body, cannot just step away).
Saying radiation always causes cancer — it increases the RISK of cancer. Many people are exposed to background radiation daily and do not develop cancer.
clozePassages: Ionising radiation is hazardous because it can damage DNA in cells, potentially causing mutations that lead to cancer. High doses can cause radiation sickness and death. The risk depends on the type of radiation, the dose received, and whether the source is inside or outside the body. Contamination (radioactive material on or in the body) is especially dangerous as exposure is prolonged. Protective measures include shielding, distance, and limiting exposure time.

Workers who handle radioactive materials are monitored using dosimeters that measure their radiation exposure. Precautions include wearing lead aprons, using remote handling equipment, and spending minimal time near sources. In medical and industrial applications, the benefits of using radiation must be weighed against the risks. Background radiation contributes to our total radiation dose throughout our lives.

The effects of radiation on the body depend on the dose and type of radiation. Low doses increase the long-term risk of cancer. High doses cause immediate cell death, leading to radiation sickness. Alpha particles are most dangerous when inhaled or ingested because they are highly ionising inside body tissues. Beta particles can cause skin burns. Gamma rays can penetrate the body and damage internal organs. Risk is reduced by using the ALARP principle — as low as reasonably practicable.

Nuclear Reactions.intro: Nuclear fission and fusion are reactions involving the nuclei of atoms that release enormous amounts of energy. Understanding both is essential for P4.
Nuclear Reactions.mnemonic: "Fission = breaking Families apart (large → small); Fusion = Friends joining together (small → large)" — fission SPLITS, fusion JOINS.

sections.title: Nuclear Fission
sections.text: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons that can trigger a chain reaction.
points: Fission — a large nucleus (e.g. uranium-235 or plutonium-239) absorbs a slow neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei
Products — two daughter nuclei + 2 or 3 neutrons + gamma radiation + large release of energy
Chain reaction — released neutrons trigger further fissions; can be controlled or uncontrolled
Controlled (power station) — control rods absorb excess neutrons; maintains steady reaction rate
Uncontrolled (weapon) — supercritical mass; neutrons multiply exponentially → explosion

sections.title: Nuclear Power Stations
sections.text: Nuclear power stations use controlled fission chain reactions to generate heat, which drives turbines and generators to produce electricity.
points: Moderator — water or graphite slows neutrons down so they can be absorbed and trigger fission
Control rods — boron rods inserted/withdrawn to absorb neutrons and control reaction rate; fully inserted = shutdown
Coolant — water (or CO₂) carries heat from reactor core to produce steam; steam drives turbines → generators
Fuel rods — uranium-235 or plutonium-239; gradually depleted and replaced
Containment — thick concrete and steel shields to prevent radiation escaping

sections.title: Nuclear Fusion
sections.text: Nuclear fusion joins small nuclei together to form a larger nucleus, releasing huge amounts of energy. It powers the Sun and stars.

callout.label: Fusion vs Fission
callout.text: Fission: large nucleus SPLITS (current nuclear power). Fusion: small nuclei JOIN (future, powers stars). Fusion releases more energy per kg and produces no long-lived radioactive waste.

points: Fusion — two hydrogen isotopes (deuterium and tritium) join to form helium + neutron + huge energy release
Powers the Sun — Sun fuses hydrogen into helium; gravitational pressure confines the plasma
Temperature barrier — requires temperatures of ~10⁷ K to overcome electrostatic repulsion between nuclei
Not yet commercial — containment of plasma (using magnetic fields in tokamak) is the main challenge
Advantages of fusion — no CO₂ emissions; fuel (hydrogen isotopes) abundant; much less radioactive waste than fission

keyTerms.def: A large nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits into smaller nuclei, releasing energy and more neutrons
Fission reactions where neutrons released trigger further fissions — can be controlled or uncontrolled
Small nuclei (hydrogen isotopes) join together to form a larger nucleus, releasing enormous energy
Boron rods in a reactor that absorb neutrons to control the rate of fission
Material (water or graphite) that slows neutrons so they can trigger further fission
A high-temperature state of matter where electrons are stripped from nuclei — required for fusion

examTips: Fission = SPLITS (uranium). Fusion = JOINS (hydrogen). Both release energy but by opposite processes. A very common AQA exam question asks you to distinguish between them.
Fusion is better (more energy, cleaner) but requires impossibly high temperatures — the challenge is containment. Magnetic confinement (tokamak) is used in research reactors like ITER.
Control rods control the reaction rate by absorbing neutrons; the moderator SLOWS neutrons so they can be absorbed. These are two different functions — do not confuse them.
commonMistakes: Confusing fission (large nucleus splits) and fusion (small nuclei join) — these are opposite processes.
Saying fusion is already used in power stations — it is NOT yet commercially viable; only fission is used in current nuclear power plants.
Saying control rods slow down the neutrons — control rods ABSORB neutrons; the moderator slows them. Different roles.
clozePassages: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large, unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei, releasing large amounts of energy and two or three neutrons. These neutrons can cause further fission reactions in a chain reaction. In a nuclear power station, the chain reaction is controlled using control rods that absorb neutrons. The energy released heats water to produce steam, which drives turbines connected to generators.

Nuclear fusion is the joining of two small nuclei to form a larger one, releasing enormous amounts of energy. It is the process that powers the Sun. Fusion requires extremely high temperatures (millions of degrees) to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between nuclei. On Earth, scientists are working on fusion reactors that could provide a clean, virtually unlimited energy source. ITER is an international fusion experiment aiming to demonstrate the feasibility of fusion power.

Nuclear fission and fusion both convert a small amount of mass into a large amount of energy, as described by Einstein's equation E = mc². Fission produces radioactive waste that remains hazardous for thousands of years. Fusion produces much less radioactive waste and uses hydrogen isotopes as fuel, which are abundant. The main challenge for fusion power is maintaining the extremely high temperatures and pressures needed to sustain the reaction in a plasma.
